h1: Hop water, kombucha or alcohol-free beer: picking your first product
title: Choosing Your First Alcohol-Free Drink | Craft Beer School
desc: A founder's comparison of hop water, kombucha and alcohol-free beer: equipment, risk, licences, shelf life and which to launch first.
teaser: Three alcohol-free drinks, three very different businesses. Pick the one your kit and your team can actually run.
standfirst: Hop water, kombucha and alcohol-free beer all sit in the same fridge at the bar, but they are made in very different ways. Each has its own equipment, microbial risk and regulatory question. This guide helps you pick the first one to launch.
sections: Start with what you already have

The best first product is usually the one closest to what your team already does well. A brewery has tanks, CO2, a hop store and people who understand fermentation and sanitation. A café or food business may have a kitchen and a cold room but no brewhouse. Your answer depends on that starting point more than on any trend.

Then ask three questions of each option. What equipment does it need? What can go wrong in the can? What does the label have to say? Our overview of low and no alcohol production routes covers the technical side in more depth.

Hop water is carbonated water flavoured with hops, often with a little acid, no sugar and no alcohol. There is no fermentation, so the process is short: treat the water, add hops or hop products, adjust the acid, carbonate and package.

Why it suits a first launch: low ingredient cost, short production time and no alcohol to manage.

The catch: plain water with no alcohol, little acid and no hop bitterness to speak of offers few barriers to microbes. Producers usually acidify it, commonly with citric or lactic acid. Many also pasteurise. Hop aroma also fades fast in warm storage, so a strong cold chain matters. Flavour is subtle, so the hop choice and dose must be right.

Kombucha is sweet tea fermented by a culture of yeast and acetic acid bacteria, giving a tart, lightly fizzy drink. You need a kitchen-scale fermentation set-up, good hygiene and patience. It suits a business that likes craft and storytelling.

The catch: the yeast in kombucha makes alcohol. If the drink is sold live and unpasteurised, it can keep fermenting in the bottle and drift above the alcohol limit for a soft drink, especially in warm shops. Managing that is the central technical problem of kombucha. Batch to batch consistency is also harder than with hop water. See our guide on kombucha and water kefir production.
Alcohol-free beer: the hardest of the three

Alcohol-free beer tastes most like the beer your customers already know. It often commands the best price. It is also the hardest to make well.

There are two broad routes. You can brew a normal beer and remove the alcohol with dealcoholisation equipment, which is expensive. Or you can limit how much alcohol forms in the first place, using special yeasts that cannot ferment maltose or a mash designed to leave little fermentable sugar. That route is cheaper but often leaves a worty, sweet flavour that takes skill to manage.

The catch: alcohol-free beer has sugar, a pH that is not especially low and no alcohol, which makes it vulnerable to spoilage. Pasteurisation and very careful hygiene are close to essential.

Alcohol-free drinks in India generally fall under food regulation by FSSAI rather than state excise, but only if they stay within the alcohol limit for a non-alcoholic drink. If you also hold an excise licence for beer, ask a licensing consultant how the state wants the two products separated in production, storage and records. Rules vary and change.

Be careful with health language on any of these drinks. Words like detox or gut healing on a kombucha label can be treated as health claims that need approval or evidence.

For most breweries, hop water is the lowest risk first product. It uses kit you have, takes days rather than weeks and teaches your team how alcohol-free drinks behave in the cold chain. For a café or food business without a brewhouse, kombucha often fits better. Alcohol-free beer is the strongest product commercially, but it is usually the second launch, after you have proven your hygiene and pasteurisation on something simpler.

Whatever you choose, run small batches, put them through shelf life tests in warm conditions and only scale once the drink tastes the same in week six as in week one. Ask a few bars and shops to stock the pilot and listen to what their customers say. A drink that sells in one taproom fridge tells you more than a focus group.
faqs: Which alcohol-free drink is easiest for a brewery to make?
Hop water. It needs no fermentation, uses kit a brewery already has and has a short production time, though it still needs acidification and good hygiene.
Why is kombucha risky to sell live?
The yeast keeps working in the bottle and can push alcohol above the limit for a soft drink, especially in warm storage.
Do I need an excise licence for hop water or kombucha?
Generally not, if they stay within the alcohol limit for a non-alcoholic drink, as they then fall under food regulation. Check with a licensing consultant for your state.
Is alcohol-free beer worth it for a small brewery?
It can be the best product commercially, but it needs strong hygiene and usually pasteurisation. Many breweries launch something simpler first.
